report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is plausible and supported by evidence, but it is stronger to say that olive oil—especially when it replaces less-healthful fats within a Mediterranean-style diet—is *associated with* lower stroke risk. It is not yet proven that simply adding olive oil to any diet will prevent stroke.

A 2014 meta-analysis combining observational studies (38,673 people for stroke) found that each 25 g/day higher olive-oil intake was associated with about **26% lower stroke risk** (relative risk 0.74). Observational findings can be partly explained by confounding: people who use more olive oil may also eat more vegetables, exercise, or have other advantages.  
https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/olive-oil-consumption-and-risk-of-chd-andor-stroke-a-metaanalysis-of-casecontrol-cohort-and-intervention-studies/79A90337470271D8A8CE2FDC77BD869E

More persuasive randomized evidence comes from PREDIMED: 7,447 Spanish adults aged 55–80 at elevated cardiovascular risk were assigned to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil, the same diet with nuts, or low-fat dietary advice. Major cardiovascular events (a composite including stroke) were lower in both Mediterranean-diet groups. However, this tests a *dietary pattern plus supplementation*, not olive oil alone, and participants may not represent younger or lower-risk populations.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29897866/

A newer meta-analysis of prospective cohorts likewise reports lower cardiovascular-disease risk with greater olive-oil intake, but cohort evidence remains non-randomized.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9623257/

**Practical interpretation:** Use olive oil in place of butter, lard, or other saturated-fat-rich fats, rather than adding it on top of usual calories; pair it with an overall Mediterranean-style eating pattern and established stroke prevention measures (blood-pressure control, not smoking, physical activity).
